passages.happening:
David tells the assembly that Solomon is young and inexperienced, and ‘The task is great because this palace is not for man, but for the LORD God’ (verse 1). He has provided for the house with all his ability, and now, ‘because of my delight in the house of my God, I now give for it my personal treasures of gold and silver’ (verse 3): three thousand talents of the gold of Ophir and seven thousand of refined silver (verse 4). He asks, “Now who will volunteer to consecrate himself to the LORD today?” (verse 5).

The leaders of the households, the tribes, the commanders and the king's officials ‘gave willingly’ (verse 6): gold, including 10,000 darics, silver, bronze, iron and precious stones (verses 7-8). ‘And the people rejoiced at the willing response of their leaders, for they had given to the LORD freely and wholeheartedly. And King David also rejoiced greatly’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
This is the last scene of 1 Chronicles and the end of the handover begun in chapter 28. David has given Solomon the plan and the charge; now he gives the materials, and the nation joins him. The scene is set around 970 BC.

Kings across the ancient world boasted of the gold they lavished on their gods' houses. What stands out here is willingness. The verb nadav, to give freely or volunteer, comes seven times in the chapter, and the people's joy comes from the fact that the gifts were given freely and wholeheartedly, not from their size. The model is the tabernacle offering in Exodus, where the people brought so much willingly that Moses had to tell them to stop.

The amounts are vast; a talent was a heavy unit, often estimated at roughly thirty kilograms. Gold of Ophir was famous for its quality, though no one knows where Ophir was: southern Arabia, the East African coast and India have all been proposed. Verse 7 mentions darics, a Persian gold coin first minted around the end of the sixth century BC, some five centuries after David. The Chronicler is almost certainly giving the sum in the money his readers knew, as a modern writer might give an ancient sum in dollars. It is one of the clearest signs that Chronicles was written in the Persian period.
passages.later: At the tabernacle the people gave so freely that a proclamation went out: “No man or woman should make anything else as an offering for the sanctuary” (Exodus 36:6). Paul wrote, ‘Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver’ (2 Corinthians 9:7).
passages.asks: The people rejoiced because the giving was willing. Ask whether your giving is a joy or a weight. And ask what David's question would ask of you: who will consecrate himself to the LORD today?

passages.happening:
David praises the LORD before the assembly: ‘Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the splendor and the majesty, for everything in heaven and on earth belongs to You. Yours, O LORD, is the kingdom, and You are exalted as head over all’ (verse 11). ‘Both riches and honor come from You’ (verse 12).

‘But who am I, and who are my people, that we should be able to give as generously as this? For everything comes from You, and from Your own hand we have given to You’ (verse 14). ‘For we are foreigners and strangers in Your presence, as were all our forefathers. Our days on earth are like a shadow, without hope’ (verse 15). He prays that God will keep this desire in the hearts of his people and direct their hearts toward him (verse 18), and asks, ‘And give my son Solomon a whole heart to keep and carry out all Your commandments’ (verse 19). Then the whole assembly praises the LORD and bows down (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
The prayer is the heart of the chapter. It opens with praise that piles up words for God's greatness, turns to humble confession of how small the king and his people are, then to the brevity of human life, and ends in prayer for the people and for Solomon. Its key words are give, willing, heart and hand.

Everything given came first from God's hand. That is the logic of the whole prayer: no one can make God richer, and the gift is only returning what was his. David calls Israel foreigners and strangers, ger and toshav, people living in a land not their own, as Abraham did in Canaan. A king at the height of his power describes himself as a guest passing through. The heart, levav, in Hebrew thought is less the seat of feeling than of intention and decision; David asks God to direct the people's hearts and to give Solomon a whole one.

Many scholars think that the words added at the end of the Lord's Prayer in later manuscripts of Matthew and in early Christian worship, the kingdom and the power and the glory, echo verse 11.
passages.later: A psalm of David prays, ‘For I am a foreigner dwelling with You, a stranger like all my fathers’ (Psalm 39:12).
passages.asks: David said that everything comes from God, and that every gift to God came first from his hand. Ask what you hold as yours that is really his. And ask how it would change your days to see yourself, as David did, as a guest passing through.

passages.t: Solomon on the throne of the LORD, and David's death
passages.happening:
The next day the people offer a thousand bulls, a thousand rams and a thousand lambs, with other sacrifices in abundance (verse 21). ‘That day they ate and drank with great joy in the presence of the LORD’ (verse 22), and for a second time they make Solomon king, anointing him as ruler and Zadok as priest. ‘So Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD as king in place of his father David. He prospered, and all Israel obeyed him’ (verse 23). The officials, the mighty men and all David's sons pledge allegiance (verse 24).

‘David son of Jesse was king over all Israel’ (verse 26), for forty years, seven in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem (verse 27). ‘He died at a ripe old age, full of years, riches, and honor, and his son Solomon reigned in his place’ (verse 28). His acts are written in the records of Samuel the seer, Nathan the prophet and Gad the seer (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
The burnt offerings were wholly burned, but the other sacrifices were most likely fellowship offerings, eaten by the worshipers, which is why the day ends with eating and drinking with great joy. A second time looks back to 23:1, where David made Solomon king. First Kings 1 tells of a hurried anointing at the Gihon spring when Adonijah tried to take the throne; the Chronicler shows a public, joyful confirmation. Here all of David's sons pledge allegiance to Solomon.

Solomon sat on the throne of the LORD, one of the Chronicler's boldest phrases: the son of David rules on God's own throne. The summary of David's reign agrees with 1 Kings 2 on the forty years. The book ends with a citation of sources, a habit the Chronicler shares with Kings. The records of Samuel, Nathan and Gad have not survived as separate books.

So ends the Chronicler's David. Most of his account has been about the ark, the temple and the ordering of worship, and it closes the same way: the king's last public act is an offering and a prayer. Second Chronicles will open with Solomon established and ready to build.
passages.later: First Kings says, ‘Then David rested with his fathers and was buried in the City of David’ (1 Kings 2:10), and gives the same years: ‘seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem’ (1 Kings 2:11).
passages.asks: David died full of years, riches and honor, and the last thing he did in public was give and pray. Ask what you want the last things people saw of you to be. And ask what you are building now that someone after you will finish.
